headline: Your child may have $1,000 waiting in a Trump Account. Here’s how to claim it.

sources.excerpt: More than 60 million children were automatically registered for “Trump Accounts,” and some of those children have $1,000 in the accounts waiting to be claimed. Here’s what you need to know about claiming the cash for your child. “Trump Accounts,” or 530A accounts, function similarly to an individual retirement account. Every U.S. citizen under the age of eighteen with a social security number is eligible for an account. Anyone can make contributions to the account, up to $5,000 for individuals and $2,500 for employers contributing to their workers’ children’s accounts. Government entities and charities can also make contributions. The money placed in the accounts will be invested in the stock market, and children can remove the money on Jan. 1 of the year they turn 18 or roll it into a retirement account. However, there are penalties if the money is withdrawn before age 59 1/2. Any taxable earnings withdrawn early are subject to income tax plus a 10% penalty. There are some exceptions for buying a home or expenses for higher education. On Oct. 1, the U.S. Treasury Department announced it had auto-enrolled all U.S. children under 18. The parents, however, still need to set up the accounts. Children born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028 will have an automatic $1,000 in their account from the U.S. Treasury Department. If your child is older, they may still be able to get some money: Children born from 2016 to 2024 that live in a ZIP code where the median household income is below $150,000 can get $250 from Michael and Susan Dell, billionaires who pledged $6.25 billion to the program. Even though children were auto-enrolled in the program, parents still need to go to ⁨trumpaccounts.gov⁩, download an app and fill out an IRS form 4547. The form asks for information like the child’s social security number, the guardian’s social security number and the name of the hospital where the child was born, as written on the birth certificate. As a parent goes through the process, they also need to take a photo of their drivers license and the app will make them scan their face as a security measure. It takes 1-3 days for the form to process. Many parents were missing out. Only 5% of low- and moderate-income homes eligible for Trump Accounts actually enrolled, according to a study by Commonwealth, a nonprofit. The top barriers for the families were the impact on taxes, inability to contribute funds and lack of trust in the Trump administration. Parents don’t have to choose to open the Trump account. Just because a child was auto-enrolled doesn’t mean the account is open, parents still have to submit the IRS form and download the app. U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent will be in Pennsylvania Monday to discuss Trump Accounts at a press conference with Pennsylvania lawmakers.

Millions of children have now been automatically enrolled in Trump accounts as part of new rules rolled out by the Treasury Department, officials have confirmed. The department said last month that accounts would be created for more than 60 million children. The move was, in part, to allow a $6.25 billion contribution pledge from Michael Dell to reach more eligible children, The Hill reported in September. Prior to the auto-enrollment, Trump accounts had been established for roughly 7 million children. As many as 70 million may qualify, according to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. “This is a transformative milestone in the Trump Administration’s effort to give every American child the opportunity to build generational wealth and jump-start their financial future,” Bessent said in a press release. Here’s what to know if your child has been automatically enrolled. If you did not previously register your child for a Trump account, either online or via your taxes, and they’re among the more than 60 million children that have been automatically enrolled, you will need to claim the account before contributions can be made. To do so, according to the Treasury Department, you’ll need to download the Trump Accounts app, which is available for iOS and Android devices. There, you will have to verify your identity and relationship to the child, review their information, and accept account terms. If your child additionally qualifies for a $1,000 one-time contribution from the Treasury Department, you will still need to establish their account and request the seed money. These funds are only available for children born between January 1, 2025, and December 31, 2028. Any U.S. child with a Social Security number who is under the age of 18 qualifies for a Trump account. If their Social Security card reads “Valid for Work Only with DHS Authorization,” the IRS says their Social Security number is considered “valid only as long as the DHS authorization is valid.” The age of your child and where you live will also impact whether or not they receive seed funds to kickstart their account. Millions qualify for at least $250 in seed money. Essentially anyone, though there are limits on certain contributions. Seed funds from the local, state or federal government, as well as philanthropic efforts, can be added to accounts. These funds do not count toward contribution caps. Contributions can also come from you, friends, family and other adults, though these funds have a $5,000 annual cap. Your employer can make contributions, with an annual cap of $2,500, which counts against the aforementioned $5,000. Previously announced employer contributions from several companies are also available. These caps will be adjusted yearly based on inflation, the IRS said. When your child turns 18, they can use the accrued funds for education costs, a home purchase or to start a business. There may be additional tax on early distributions from the account, and the IRS notes that there may be exceptions “such as for distributions for higher education expenses or first home purchases.” Like retirement accounts, this will vary. Let’s say you start an account for your child, who is eligible to receive the $1,000 seed funds from the Treasury, but no additional contributions are made. If the S&P 500 continues its annual growth rate of 10.5%, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent previously predicted the account could grow to roughly $600,000 by the time your child reaches retirement age. An analysis by the Council of Economic Advisers suggested the account of a child born in 2026 could be worth more than $300,000 by the time they turn 18 if the maximum annual contributions are made. By 28, the account could be worth more than $1 million, under a high-yield scenario. The IRS explains that the “growth period” for the accounts will end on Dec. 31 of the year before the child turns 18.
